Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
I've read it. Here is a summary of the report, my assessment, the issues worth raising, and how it changes the picture across the five papers.

## What the report says

**Varden case-processing offices at 24 months** (7 treated v 7 control, randomised, administrative output):

| Measure | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per hour (timesheets) | +12.5% | +9.8% |
| Output per hour (system logs, new) | — | +8.5% (CI 3.4 to 13.8) |
| Output per employee | −2.1% | −3.4% (CI −8.0 to +1.2) |

Appeal overturns, sick days and resignations held roughly steady. Logs recorded slightly more work than timesheets.

**Registered mediation analysis** (filed at month 11, before the 24-month outcomes):

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain |
|---|---|
| Fewer recurring meetings | 47% (CI 28 to 66) |
| Reduced fatigue | 18% (CI 2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

Meeting time in treated offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours a week. Control offices went from 7.2 to 7.0.

**An unplanned observation:** two control offices ran their own "meeting audit" at month 15. Their output per hour rose 4.1% against their own previous six months, with hours unchanged. The authors label this as suggestive only.

**Counter arm:** the county ended it at month 12. Waits were 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and restoring service would need 12% more staff, raising cost per contact by about 9%.

**Halden follow-up:** 14 of the 23 organisations with records responded.
- Three reverted: hospitality, retail, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines.
- The 11 that continued show output at 96.8 and a per-hour gain of +11.8%. The authors correctly call this an upper bound from organisations selected twice: once by finishing the pilot, once by choosing to continue.

**Bearing on earlier claims:**
- The comment's "entirely an artifact" is not supported. The 8.5% gain survives the very standards the comment recommended.
- The review's "no decay" claim rested on four long studies that were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. In the one controlled long study, the gain declined by about a quarter.

## Overall assessment

This is a careful follow-up, and most of its claims are stated at about the right weight.

What it gets right:
- It registered the mediation test before seeing the outcomes.
- It added a stricter measure of hours.
- It labels the Halden subset as an upper bound.
- It reports the meeting-audit observation together with the reasons it can't establish anything.

It also resolves several points I raised earlier:
- **Meeting baselines:** they are now reported (7.4 v 7.2), so the month-six gap was not a pre-existing imbalance.
- **Counter waiting times:** now compared against control.
- **Counter cost:** now estimated.
- **The review's duration claim:** shown to rest on four uncontrolled, scheduled-hours studies, confirming the concern I raised.

It is worth saying explicitly: this report agrees with much of what I said before, and that is a reason to check it more carefully, not less.

I checked the arithmetic:

| Calculation | Result | Holds? |
|---|---|---|
| 0.966 / 0.88 | +9.8% | ✓ |
| 0.966 / 0.89 | +8.5% | ✓ |
| Halden subset hours: 34.9 / 40.3 | −13.4% | ✓ |
| Halden subset per hour: 96.8 / 0.866 | +11.8% | ✓ |
| Mediation shares: 47 + 18 + 35 | 100 | ✓ |
| Restoring counter service: 1 / (0.83 × 1.067) | about 13% more staff | ✓ (report says 12%) |

## Issues

**1. It's unclear what the log-hours measure captures, and this bears on the headline and the mediation.**
The measure is "active log-in time on the county's case-management system," described as time spent working on cases. Meetings presumably don't happen in that system.

If logs exclude meetings, the numbers are hard to reconcile:
- Treated timesheet hours fell by about 4.5 hours a week, and meeting time fell by 3.5 hours.
- So non-meeting time fell by only about 1 hour, roughly 3%.
- Log hours should then fall by about 3% relative to control, not 11%.

That leaves two possibilities:
- **Logs include meeting time**, for example because staff stay logged in. Then the measure isn't case work time, and "logs show slightly more work than timesheets" means something different from what the report implies.
- **Logs exclude meetings.** Then cutting meetings can't raise output per log hour simply by freeing up time. A 47% mediation share would have to work through a less direct channel, such as less fragmented focus. That would be an interesting finding, but it needs stating and the numbers above need reconciling.

Either way, the report should define the measure and show how meetings fit into it. The headline 8.5% and the mediation result both depend on it.

**2. The control offices' meeting audit contaminates the comparison and may account for part of the "decline."**
Two of the seven control offices raised their output per hour by about 4% from month 15. That lifts the control average by roughly 1 point, which shrinks the measured treatment effect by about the same.

So of the 12.5 → 9.8 decline, perhaps a point or so reflects controls improving rather than treated offices fading. That is a rough estimate on my part. The report treats the audit only as evidence that gains might come without cutting hours. It also matters for the decay estimate, and the report should say so. Re-estimating with those two offices excluded, or with the comparison ending at month 15, would show how much.

There is a related point. If the audit was prompted by watching treated colleagues, that is spillover, which office-level randomisation was meant to prevent.

**3. The summary overstates both the decline and the mediation result.**
- **Decline:** "fell from 12.5% to 8.5%" compares a timesheet figure at 9 months with a log figure at 24 months. The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% to 9.8%. Even that is not statistically established, because the confidence intervals overlap heavily (6.9 to 18.4 against 4.6 to 15.2). The body's "consistent with some fading" is the right wording; the summary should match it.
- **Mediation:** "A registered mediation test *confirms*" is stronger than the limitations section, which notes that mediation assumes no unmeasured confounding. Meeting cuts weren't randomised. Offices with better managers might both cut more meetings and improve output for other reasons. "Supports" would match the evidence.

**4. The mediation analysis needs more detail on precision and independence.**
- **Sample size:** "a larger sample of office-months" adds data points, but the 14 offices are what was randomised. A 28–66% confidence interval looks narrow for 14 clusters. Confirm the standard errors are clustered by office.
- **Independence:** the test was registered before the 24-month data, which is real protection. But the hypothesis came from the same seven treated offices at month six. This is a prospective test on the same units, not an independent replication. That answers the comment's "post hoc" charge in part, not fully.

**5. Two points from the nine-month report are still not addressed for case-processing.**
- **Backlog:** there is still no measure of backlog or time to decision. Over 24 months, deferring work to keep closure counts up would be easier to sustain than over nine months.
- **Cost:** the cost of overtime per case is still not reported, though the counter arm now gets a cost estimate.

**6. The Halden subset has a further layer of selection.**
Only 14 of the 23 organisations responded, on top of the two layers the authors already name. The reverting marketing agency is worth noting: it is nominally discretionary work, but client deadlines behave like coverage obligations. That supports the review's own caveat that classifying work type as one or the other is crude.

## Where the evidence now stands, across all five papers

**Well supported:**
- Scheduled hours, manager-reported output and uncontrolled designs each inflate estimates.
- In coverage-bound work, cutting hours without hiring reduces output and service. Restoring service costs about 9% more per contact in the one costed case, and the county ended its own arm.
- Per-hour gains are not entirely an artifact.

**Moderately supported:**
- In discretionary work, output per actual hour rises by about 8–10%, and the gain persists to 24 months in the one controlled long-run study.
- Output per employee is slightly below control there (−3.4%, CI −8.0 to +1.2).

**Partly answered, which is the main change:**
- **Durability:** there is now within-study evidence. Some fading is plausible, but part of it may be contamination of the controls, and it rests on one employer with 7 v 7 offices.
- **Mechanism:** cutting meetings is now the leading candidate, with support from a registered test, and fatigue plays a smaller role. This depends on clarifying the log-hours measure and on no unmeasured confounding.

**Open:**
- whether reorganising alone, without cutting hours, captures most of the gain (the meeting audit hints yes, but no arm tested it)
- whether the findings transfer beyond one public employer
- cost and backlog in discretionary work
- how much attrition biased the Halden results

The open question about reorganisation without an hours cut is now the most policy-relevant one. A trial with a "meeting audit, no hours change" arm would answer it directly.

I can draft a referee report for this paper or update the evidence brief.
